## Appendix E Exactness of the Unadjusted cPCH Test under the Least Favorable Null Case

We first discuss the behavior of the cPCH test under the least favorable null case, which we introduced in Section 1.3 as the setting where, informally, there are exactly $r-1$ $\theta_{i}$ ’s with $\left|\theta_{i}\right|$ equaling infinity. In this section, we formalize this initial description and prove a validity result for the unadjusted cPCH test under the least favorable null case.

First, we provide some intuition for the least favorable null case. As discussed in Section 2.1, the data for each base hypothesis is commonly summarized as an asymptotically normal parameter estimator such as a sample mean or ordinary least squares coefficient. Under our assumed setting in Section 2.1, we expect the non-null $T_{i}$ ’s under fixed alternatives to approach infinity in magnitude as their underlying sample size approaches infinity. For example, if each base hypothesis test reports a sample mean of $n$ i.i.d. observations each approximated by a $\mathcal{N}(\mu_{i},1)$ distribution, then the standard $z$ -test statistic is $T_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\theta_{i},1)$ where $\theta_{i}=\sqrt{n}\mu_{i}$ . Therefore, as $n$ approaches infinity, the non-null $\left|\theta_{i}\right|$ ’s will also approach infinity, and thus, so will their corresponding $\left|T_{i}\right|$ ’s.

When the base test statistics are independent and the null base p-values are uniformly distributed, the standard Fisher and Simes single PCH test are exact tests under the least favorable null case. We show that the unadjusted cPCH test exhibits a similar property under the least favorable null case. First, we formalize our initial description of the least favorable null case by defining an least favorable null sequence:

#### Definition 3 (Least Favorable Null Sequence).

An least favorable null sequence $(\bm{\theta}^{(n)})$ is a sequence in $\Theta_{0}^{r/m}$ such that $\left|\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(j)}\right|\to\infty$ for $j=m-r+2,...,m$ as $n\to\infty$ .

We will prove that, under the least favorable null case, the limiting Type I error of the following more general version of the unadjusted cPCH test (for any m) is exactly $\alpha$ as $n\to\infty$ .

#### Definition 4 (Generalized cPCH test).

The generalized cPCH test rejects $H_{0}^{r/m}$ when

$f\left(\bm{T}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)>c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)$ .

In particular, Assumption 3 allows for more general sequences of estimators for $\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}$ when setting the rejection threshold of the unadjusted cPCH test. Setting $\hat{\bm{\theta}}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}_{(m-r+2:m)}$ recovers the original cPCH test as in Definition 2.

Let $\bm{T}^{(n)}$ denote a test statistic vector, with the superscript $(n)$ now allowing us to vary $\bm{T}^{(n)}$ ’s distribution. Let $\varphi^{\text{ucPCH}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\coloneqq\mathbbm{1}\left\{f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)>c_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\right\}$ and $\varphi^{\text{PCHOrac}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\coloneqq\mathbbm{1}\left\{f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)>c_{\alpha}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\right\}$ denote the decisions made by the unadjusted cPCH test and PCH Oracle test, respectively. Throughout all proofs, we will use “ $\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\to}}$ ” to denote convergence in probability and the superscript “c” to denote the complement of a set.

#### Assumption 1.

Assume $\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)}\right)$ is a LFN sequence and that $\bm{T}^{(n)}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},I_{m})$ .

#### Assumption 2.

Assume $f:\mathbb{R}^{m-r+1}\to\mathbb{R}$ is permutation invariant, continuously differentiable, and has $\gradient f\neq 0$ except on a set whose closure has measure zero.

#### Assumption 3.

Assume $\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)$ is a sequence of estimators for the LFN sequence $\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)$ with the following property: For any $K>0$ , $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(i)}\right|>K\right)=1$ for $i=m-r+2,...,m$ .

#### Theorem 1 (Exactness of the unadjusted cPCH test under the least favorable null case).

Under Assumptions 1–3, for any $\alpha\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\varphi^{\text{cPCH}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)=\varphi^{\text{PCHOrac}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right)=1. $$

In particular, the above implies that the generalized cPCH test’s limiting Type I error under any LFN sequence is exactly $\alpha$ .

Theorem 1 shows not only that the unadjusted cPCH test achieves exactly the nominal Type I error rate in the least favorable null case, but that it in fact behaves identically to the PCH Oracle test in such a case. Note as well that the Fisher and Simes combining functions satisfy the conditions on $f$ specified in the theorem statement. The proof is provided below.

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality, assume $\bm{\theta}^{(n)}=\left(0,...0,\theta^{(n)}_{m-r+2},...,\theta^{(n)}_{m}\right)$ where $\theta^{(n)}_{i}\to\infty$ for $i=m-r+2,...,m$ . Let $R_{f}\coloneqq\text{Range}(f)$ . For $x\in R_{f}$ , let $G\left(x,\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\coloneqq\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x\right)$ .33 3 By Assumption 2, $G$ is permutation invariant with respect to $\bm{\theta}^{(n)}$ , so $\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x\right)=\mathbb{P}_{\sigma(\bm{\theta}^{(n)})}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x\right)$ for any permutation of the elements of $\bm{\theta}^{(n)}$ , $\sigma(\bm{\theta}^{(n)})$ . Therefore, we can use $\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}$ to represent $\bm{\theta}^{(n)}$ in the input to $G$ . Let $H(x)\coloneqq\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{1:m-r+1}\right)\leq x\right)$ ; note that $\bm{T}^{(n)}_{1:m-r+1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},I_{m-r+1})$ for all $n$ , so $H$ does not vary with $n$ . For $a\in(0,1)$ , let

$c_{a}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)=\inf\left\{x:G\left(x,\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\geq 1-a\right\}$ and $c_{a}^{*}=\inf\left\{x:H(x)\geq 1-a\right\}$ .

Lemma 1 (stated below and proved in Supplementary Material F) establishes that $c_{\alpha}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)$ , the rejection threshold of the level $\alpha$ PCH Oracle test, converges to $c_{\alpha}^{*}$ :

#### Lemma 1.

Under Assumptions 1-2, for $\alpha\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ c_{\alpha}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\to c_{\alpha}^{*}. $$

Lemma 2 (stated below and proved in Supplementary Material F) establishes that

$c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)$ , the rejection threshold of the level $\alpha$ generalized cPCH test, converges to $c_{\alpha}^{*}$ in probability:44 4 Unlike $c_{\alpha}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)$ , which is a fixed real number for each $n$ , $c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)$ is a random variable that is a function of $\bm{T}^{(n)}$ both through the conditioning event and $\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}$ .

#### Lemma 2.

Under Assumptions 1-3, for $\alpha\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\to}}c_{\alpha}^{*}. $$

Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $\epsilon>0$ . Let $Q_{n}=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(|c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)-c_{\alpha}^{*}|\leq\epsilon\right)$ . By Lemma 2, $\lim_{n\to\infty}Q_{n}=1$ . So,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\varphi^{\text{cPCH}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\neq\varphi^{\text{PCHOrac}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\varphi^{\text{cPCH}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\neq\varphi^{\text{PCHOrac}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\;\middle|\;|c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)-c_{\alpha}^{*}|\leq\epsilon\right)Q_{n}+ \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\varphi^{\text{cPCH}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\neq\varphi^{\text{PCHOrac}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\;\middle|\;|c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)-c_{\alpha}^{*}|>\epsilon\right)(1-Q_{n}) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\varphi^{\text{cPCH}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\neq\varphi^{\text{PCHOrac}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\;\middle|\;|c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)-c_{\alpha}^{*}|\leq\epsilon\right), $$

where the last line follows from Lemma 2. By Lemma 1, there exists $N_{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n\geq N_{\epsilon}$ , $|c_{\alpha}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)-c_{\alpha}^{*}|<\epsilon$ . So, for $n\geq N_{\epsilon}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\varphi^{\text{cPCH}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\neq\varphi^{\text{PCHOrac}}_{\alpha}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\;\middle|\;|c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)-c_{\alpha}^{*}|\leq\epsilon\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\in\left(c_{\alpha}^{*}-\epsilon,c_{\alpha}^{*}+\epsilon\right)\;\middle|\;|c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)-c_{\alpha}^{*}|\leq\epsilon\right). $$

Since $\lim_{n\to\infty}Q_{n}=1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\in\left(c_{\alpha}^{*}-\epsilon,c_{\alpha}^{*}+\epsilon\right)\;\middle|\;|c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)-c_{\alpha}^{*}|\leq\epsilon\right) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\in\left(c_{\alpha}^{*}-\epsilon,c_{\alpha}^{*}+\epsilon\right)\right) $$

where the last line follows by Lemma 3, (stated below and proved in Supplementary Materials F), assuming the above limit exists, which we show in Equation (10):

#### Lemma 3.

Let $\left(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}\right)$ be a probability space. where the fourth line follows from the fact that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right)=1$ and the fifth line follows from the conditioning on $B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ and the permutation invariance of $f$ in Assumption 2. #### Proof.

As in Theorem 1, let $\bm{\theta}^{(n)}=\left(0,...,0,\theta_{m-r+2}^{(n)},...,\theta_{m}^{(n)}\right)$ where $\theta^{(n)}_{i}\to\infty$ and define $B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ as the event that, for $\bm{T}^{(n)}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},I_{m})$ , $\left\{T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)},...,T^{(n)}_{(m)}\right\}=\left\{T^{(n)}_{m-r+2},...,T^{(n)}_{m}\right\}$ . We will first show that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right)=1$ . Let $K>0$ . Then, for $m-r+2\leq i\leq m$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|T^{(n)}_{i}\right|>K\right)=\lim_{n\to\infty}1-\Phi\left(K-\theta^{(n)}_{i}\right)+\Phi\left(-K-\theta^{(n)}_{i}\right)=1, $$

where the last line follows from Assumption 1. Let $F^{(n)}_{K}\coloneqq\left\{\min_{i=m-r+2,...,m}\left|T^{(n)}_{i}\right|>K\right\}$ . Then,

$$ \mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(F^{(n)}_{K}\right)=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\bigcap_{i=m-r+2}^{m}\left\{\left|T^{(n)}_{i}\right|>K\right\}\right)=\prod_{i=m-r+2}^{m}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|T^{(n)}_{i}\right|>K\right)\to 1, $$

where the second equality follows from the fact that $T^{(n)}_{m-r+2},...,T^{(n)}_{m}$ are independent and the last result follows from Equation (11). So,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left\{T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)},...,T^{(n)}_{(m)}\right\}=\left\{T^{(n)}_{m-r+2},...,T^{(n)}_{m}\right\}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\max_{j=1,...,m-r+1}\left|T^{(n)}_{j}\right|<\min_{i=m-r+2,...,m}\left|T^{(n)}_{i}\right|\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\max_{j=1,...,m-r+1}\left|T^{(n)}_{j}\right|<\min_{i=m-r+2,...,m}\left|T^{(n)}_{i}\right|\;\middle|\;F^{(n)}_{K}\right)\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(F^{(n)}_{K}\right) \displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\max_{j=1,...,m-r+1}\left|T^{(n)}_{j}\right|<\min_{i=m-r+2,...,m}\left|T^{(n)}_{i}\right|\;\middle|\;F^{(n)c}_{K}\right)\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(F^{(n)c}_{K}\right). $$

By Equation (12),

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\max_{j=1,...,m-r+1}\left|T^{(n)}_{j}\right|<\min_{i=m-r+2,...,m}\left|T^{(n)}_{i}\right|\;\middle|\;F^{(n)}_{K}\right), $$

where, for any $n$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\max_{j=1,...,m-r+1}\left|T^{(n)}_{j}\right|<\min_{i=m-r+2,...,m}\left|T^{(n)}_{i}\right|\;\middle|\;F^{(n)}_{K}\right) \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\max_{j=1,...,m-r+1}\left|T^{(n)}_{j}\right|<K\;\middle|\;F^{(n)}_{K}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\max_{j=1,...,m-r+1}\left|T^{(n)}_{j}\right|<K\right) \displaystyle=(\Phi(K)-\Phi(-K))^{m-r+1}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right)\geq(\Phi(K)-\Phi(-K))^{m-r+1}. $$

Since $K$ was arbitrary, the above line holds for any $K>0$ . Note that as $K$ gets arbitrarily large, $(\Phi(K)-\Phi(-K))^{m-r+1}\to 1$ . Therefore,

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right)=1. $$

Let $x\in R_{f}$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}G\left(x,\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x\right) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x\;\middle|\;B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right)\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right)+ \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x\;\middle|\;B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)^{c}\right)\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)^{c}\right) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x\;\middle|\;B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{1:m-r+1}\right)\leq x\;\middle|\;B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\right) \displaystyle=H(x), $$

where the fourth line follows from Equation (13), and the fifth line follows from the conditioning on $B_{n}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ and the permutation invariance of $f$ in Assumption 2. The last line follows from Lemma 3 using Equation (13) and the fact that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}_{1:m-r+1}\right)\leq x\right)=H(x)$ .

So,

$$ G\left(x,\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\to H(x). $$

Since $x$ was arbitrary, the above is true for any $x\in R_{f}$ . Additionally, $H$ is continuous on $R_{f}$ as a result of Lemma 4, where $f$ satisfies the conditions of Lemma 4 by Assumption 2. Therefore, by Lemma 21.2 of van der Vaart (1998), for any $\alpha\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ c_{\alpha}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\to c_{\alpha}^{*}. $$

### F.2 Proof of Lemma 2

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality, let $\bm{\theta}^{(n)}=\left(0,...,0,\theta^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)},...,\theta^{(n)}_{(m)}\right)$ where $\theta^{(n)}_{i}\to\infty$ and let $\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}=\left(0,...,0,\hat{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)},...,\hat{\theta}^{(n)}_{(m)}\right)$ . Let

$\tilde{F}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\coloneqq\mathbb{P}_{\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\sim\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x\;\middle|\;\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ represent the probability that $f\left(\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x$ conditional on $\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}$ and $\bm{T}^{(n)}$ where the subscript on the probability denotes that $\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\mid\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\sim\mathcal{N}(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},I_{m})$ . Note, this probability is only over $\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}$ , which is a function of $\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}$ . Therefore, $\tilde{F}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ is a random variable since it is a function of $\bm{T}^{(n)}$ both through the conditioning event and through $\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}$ . We consider $\tilde{F}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ because $c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)=\inf\left\{x:\tilde{F}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\geq 1-\alpha\right\}$ . Thus, to show our final result, we will first show that, for any $x\in R_{f}$ , $\tilde{F}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\to}}H(x)$ .

Showing $\tilde{F}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\to}}H(x)$ relies on Lemma 5 (stated below and proved in Supplementary Materials F.5):

#### Lemma 5.

Under Assumptions 1 and 3,

$$ \mathbb{P}_{\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\sim\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right)\;\middle|\;\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\to}}1. $$

Here, $B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right)$ represents the event that, for $\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\mid\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\sim\mathcal{N}(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},I_{m})$ ,

$\left\{\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)},...,\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{(m)}\right\}=\left\{\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{m-r+2},...,\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{m}\right\}$ . The set $\left\{\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)},...,\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{(m)}\right\}$ will almost surely be uniquely defined since the $\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{i}$ ’s will almost surely have no ties.

Note, $\mathbb{P}_{\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\sim\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right)\;\middle|\;\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ is also a random variable as it is a function of $\bm{T}^{(n)}$ both through the conditioning event and through $\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}$ . For ease of notation, let

$\tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\coloneqq\mathbb{P}_{\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\sim\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x\;\middle|\;B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right),\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ , and let $P_{B}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)=\mathbb{P}_{\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\sim\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right)\;\middle|\;\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ and analogously, $P_{B}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)^{c}=\mathbb{P}_{\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\sim\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}}\left(B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right)^{c}\;\middle|\;\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ . Fix $x\in R_{f}$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{F}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right) \displaystyle=\tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)P_{B}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)+ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\sim\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(1:m-r+1)}\right)\leq x\;\middle|\;B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right)^{c},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)P_{B}\left(\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)^{c}. $$

Note the second term in the summation above converges in probability to $0$ by Lemma 5 and the fact $P_{B}(\bm{T}^{(n)})^{c}$ is a bounded random variable.

We will now show that $\tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\to}}H(x)$ . By the conditioning on $B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right)$ and the permutation invariance of $f$ in Assumption 2,

$$ \tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)=\mathbb{P}_{\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\sim\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}}\left(f\left(\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{1:m-r+1}\right)\leq x\;\middle|\;B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right),\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right). $$

$\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{1},...,\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{m-r+1}$ are i.i.d. standard normally distributed by assumption, so,

$$ \tilde{T}^{(n)}_{1},...,\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{m-r+1}\mid B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right),\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i.i.d.}}{{\sim}}\text{Trunc--Norm}\left(0,1,T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right), $$

where $\text{Trunc--Norm}(0,1,c)$ is the standard normal distribution truncated at $-|c|$ and $|c|$ for $c\in\mathbb{R}$ . Let $p_{\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\sim\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}}\left(\bm{t}\;\middle|\;B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right),\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ be the PDF of $\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{1},...,\tilde{T}^{(n)}_{m-r+1}$ conditional on $B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right),\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}$ evaluated at $\bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m-r+1}$ . By definition of a truncated normal random variable, we have for any $\bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m-r+1}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle p_{\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\sim\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}}\left(\bm{t}\;\middle|\;B_{n}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)},\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}\right),\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)= \displaystyle\qquad\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\frac{\phi(t_{i})\mathbbm{1}_{T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}}\left(t_{i}\right)}{\Phi\left(\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\right)-\Phi\left(-\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\right)}, $$

where $\mathbbm{1}_{T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}}\left(t\right)\coloneqq\mathbbm{1}\left\{{t\in\left(-\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|,\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\right)}\right\}$ for $t\in\mathbb{R}$ .

Set $\epsilon>0$ and define $S_{x}=\{\bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m-r+1}:f(\bm{t})<x\}$ . By Assumption 2, where the $\nabla f\neq 0$ condition guarantees the montonicity of $f$ , there exists $K_{x}>0$ such that for any $\bm{t}\in S_{x}$ , $|t_{i}|<K_{x}$ for all $i=1,...,m-r+1$ . So, for any $K_{x}>0$ satisfying this condition,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(|\tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)-H(x)|>\epsilon\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(|\tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)-H(x)|>\epsilon\;\middle|\;\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|>K_{x}\right)\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|>K_{x}\right)+ \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(|\tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)-H(x)|>\epsilon\;\middle|\;\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\leq K_{x}\right)\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\leq K_{x}\right) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(|\tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)-H(x)|>\epsilon\;\middle|\;\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|>K_{x}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|\int_{S_{x}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\frac{\phi(t_{i})\mathbbm{1}_{T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}}\left(t_{i}\right)}{\Phi\left(\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\right)-\Phi\left(-\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\right)}-\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\phi(t_{i})\right)d\bm{t}\right|>\epsilon\;\middle|\;\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|>K_{x}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|\int_{S_{x}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\frac{\phi(t_{i})}{\Phi\left(\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\right)-\Phi\left(-\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\right)}-\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\phi(t_{i})\right)d\bm{t}\right|>\epsilon\;\middle|\;\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|>K_{x}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\int_{S_{x}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\frac{\phi(t_{i})}{\Phi\left(\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\right)-\Phi\left(-\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|\right)}-\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\phi(t_{i})\right)d\bm{t}>\epsilon\;\middle|\;\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|>K_{x}\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\int_{S_{x}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\frac{\phi(t_{i})}{\Phi(K_{x})-\Phi(-K_{x})}-\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\phi(t_{i})\right)d\bm{t}>\epsilon\;\middle|\;\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|>K_{x}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\int_{S_{x}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\frac{\phi(t_{i})}{\Phi(K_{x})-\Phi(-K_{x})}-\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\phi(t_{i})\right)d\bm{t}>\epsilon\right) \displaystyle=\mathbbm{1}\left\{\left(\frac{1}{\Phi(K_{x})-\Phi(-K_{x})}-1\right)^{m-r+1}\int_{S_{x}}\prod_{i=1}^{m-r+1}\phi(t_{i})d\bm{t}>\epsilon\right\} \displaystyle=\mathbbm{1}\left\{\left(\frac{1}{\Phi(K_{x})-\Phi(-K_{x})}-1\right)^{m-r+1}H(x)>\epsilon\right\}. $$

In the third line, we drop the indicator in the numerator because of the conditioning on $\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|>K_{x}$ . The fourth line follows because the expression within the absolute value is non-negative almost surely. Note, there exists $K_{0}>0$ such that for all $K>K_{0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(K)-\Phi(-K)>\frac{1}{1+\left(\frac{\epsilon}{H(x)}\right)^{\frac{1}{m-r+1}}} $$

and therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{\Phi(K)-\Phi(-K)}-1\right)^{m-r+1}H(x)<\left(\frac{\epsilon}{H(x)}\right)H(x)=\epsilon. $$

For any $K_{x}$ satisfying $|t_{i}|<K_{x}$ for any $\bm{t}\in S_{x}$ , any $K>K_{x}$ also satisfies this condition. Therefore, we can set $K_{x}$ sufficiently large such that it satisfies this condition and Equation (16). Therefore, for such a $K_{x}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(|\tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)-H(x)|>\epsilon\;\middle|\;\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|>K_{x}\right)=0 $$

As a result of Lemma 6 (stated below and proved in Supplementary Materials F.6), for any $K>0$ , $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|T^{(n)}_{(m-r+2)}\right|>K\right)=1$ :

#### Lemma 6.

Under Assumption 1, $\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}=\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}$ satisfies Assumption 3.

Therefore, setting $K_{x}$ in Equation (15) sufficiently large to satisfy Equation (16) and $|t_{i}|<K_{x}$ for any $\bm{t}\in S_{x}$ , and applying Equation (17) and Lemma 6, we have that

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|\tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)-H(x)\right|>\epsilon\right)=0. $$

Since $\epsilon$ was arbitrary, we conclude that

$$ \tilde{G}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\to}}H(x). $$

Since $x$ was arbitrary, the above holds for any $x\in R_{f}$ . Combining the above result with Equation (14) and Lemma 5, we have that, for any $x\in R_{f}$ ,

$$ \tilde{F}\left(x,\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\to}}H(x). $$

To show the final result, we first note that $H$ is strictly increasing and continuous on $R_{f}$ as a result of Lemma 4, where $f$ satisfies the conditions of Lemma 4 by Assumption 2. Therefore, by Lemma 4 and the fact that Equation (18) holds for all $x\in R_{f}$ , $H(c^{*}_{\alpha})=1-\alpha$ for any $\alpha\in(0,1)$ . Set $0<\epsilon<\min(\alpha,1-\alpha)$ . Then, $H(c^{*}_{\alpha+\epsilon})=1-\alpha-\epsilon$ and $H(c^{*}_{\alpha-\epsilon})=1-\alpha+\epsilon$ . Set $\delta=\epsilon/2$ and let $\gamma>0$ . Then, by Equation (18), there exists $N_{1}\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n\geq N_{1}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|\tilde{F}\left(c^{*}_{\alpha+\epsilon},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)-(1-\alpha-\epsilon)\right|\leq\delta\right)\geq 1-\gamma $$

and there exists $N_{2}\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n\geq N_{2}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left|\tilde{F}\left(c^{*}_{\alpha-\epsilon},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)-(1-\alpha+\epsilon)\right|\leq\delta\right)\geq 1-\gamma. $$

Let $N=\max(N_{1},N_{2})$ . Then, for $n\geq N$ , $\tilde{F}\left(c^{*}_{\alpha+\epsilon},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ is contained in the interval $[1-\alpha-\frac{3\epsilon}{2},1-\alpha-\frac{\epsilon}{2}]$ and $\tilde{F}\left(c^{*}_{\alpha-\epsilon},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)$ is contained in the interval $[1-\alpha+\frac{\epsilon}{2},1-\alpha+\frac{3\epsilon}{2}]$ with probability $\geq 1-\gamma$ . Therefore, for any $n\geq N$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\in(c^{*}_{\alpha+\epsilon},c^{*}_{\alpha-\epsilon}]\right) \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(\left\{\tilde{F}\left(c^{*}_{\alpha+\epsilon},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)<1-\alpha\right\}\cap\left\{\tilde{F}\left(c^{*}_{\alpha-\epsilon},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)\geq 1-\alpha\right\}\right) \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\Big(\left\{\left|\tilde{F}\left(c^{*}_{\alpha+\epsilon},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)-(1-\alpha-\epsilon)\right|\leq\delta\right\}\cap\left\{\left|\tilde{F}\left(c^{*}_{\alpha-\epsilon},\bm{T}^{(n)}\right)-(1-\alpha+\epsilon)\right|\leq\delta\right\}\Big) \displaystyle\geq 1-\gamma $$

Since $\gamma$ was arbitrary, for $0<\epsilon<\min(\alpha,1-\alpha)$ ,

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{\bm{\theta}^{(n)}}\left(c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\in(c^{*}_{\alpha+\epsilon},c^{*}_{\alpha-\epsilon}]\right)=1. $$

Since $H$ is strictly increasing on $R_{f}$ , $c^{*}_{\alpha}$ is continuous for $\alpha\in(0,1)$ . Then, by the continuity of $c^{*}_{\alpha}$ and the fact that the above holds for any arbitrary $0<\epsilon<\min(\alpha,1-\alpha)$ , we conclude that

$$ c_{\alpha}\left(\hat{\bm{\theta}}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)},\bm{T}^{(n)}_{(m-r+2:m)}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\to}}c_{\alpha}^{*}. $$

### F.4 Proof of Lemma 4

#### Proof.

Let $\mu$ represent the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^{l}$ . Let $R_{f}=\text{Range}(f)$ . Let $x\in R_{f}$ and $P_{x}\coloneqq\{\bm{y}:\bm{y}\in f^{-1}(x)\}$ . Let $H$ represent the CDF of $f(\bm{X})$ . By the continuity of $f$ and the fact that $p_{\bm{X}}(\bm{x})>0$ for all $\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{l}$ , the CDF of $f(\bm{X})$ must be strictly increasing. Assume for the sake of contradiction that the CDF of $f(\bm{X})$ is not strictly increasing. Then, since $f$ is continuous, $R_{f}$ must be a connected set in $\mathbb{R}$ , i.e., $R_{f}$ must be an interval. Therefore, if the CDF of $f(\bm{X})$ is not strictly increasing, there exists some open interval $(a,b)\in R_{f}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(f(\bm{X})\in(a,b)\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\bm{X}\in f^{-1}\left((a,b)\right)\right) \displaystyle=\int_{\bm{x}\in f^{-1}\left((a,b)\right)}p_{\bm{X}}(\bm{x})d\mu $$

However, $\int_{\bm{x}\in f^{-1}\left((a,b)\right)}p_{\bm{X}}(\bm{x})d\mu>0$ since $p_{\bm{X}}(\bm{x})>0$ for all $\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{l}$ and $f^{-1}\left((a,b)\right)$ is some open set in $\mathbb{R}^{l}$ (since for continuous functions, the pre-image of open sets are open sets). Therefore, the CDF of $f(\bm{X})$ must be strictly increasing.

To show continuity, we will show that, for any $x\in R_{f}$ , $\mu(P_{x})=0$ . If this is true, then, for any fixed $x\in R_{f}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle 0=\mathbb{P}(\bm{X}\in P_{x}) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(\bm{X}\in f^{-1}\left((x-{1/n},x+{1/n}]\right)\right) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(f(\bm{X})\in(x-{1/n},x+{1/n}]\right) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(f(\bm{X})\leq x+{1/n}\right)-\mathbb{P}\left(f(\bm{X})\leq x-{1/n}\right) \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}H(x+{1/n})-H(x-{1/n}) $$

Let $\epsilon>0$ . The last line above implies that there exists $N$ sufficiently large such that for all $n\geq N$ , $H(x+{1/n})-H(x-{1/n})<\epsilon$ . So for any $0<\delta<1/n$ , if $x-\delta<x^{\prime}<x+\delta$ , then

$$ \displaystyle|H(x)-H(x^{\prime})| \displaystyle\leq H(x+\delta)-H(x-\delta)<H(x+{1/n})-H(x-{1/n})<\epsilon $$

where the first inequality follows from the fact that $H$ is a CDF and hence is nondecreasing. Since $\epsilon$ was arbitrary, $H$ is continuous at $x$ . Since the above holds for any $x\in R_{f}$ , $H$ is continuous at every $x\in R_{f}$ .

We will now show that, for any $x\in R_{f}$ , $\mu(P_{x})=0$ . Fix an arbitrary $x\in R_{f}$ . Let $Q=\{\bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{l}:f\text{ is not continuous at }\bm{t}\}\cup\{\bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{l}:f\text{ is not differentiable at }\bm{t}\}\cup\{\bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{l}:\gradient{f}\text{ is not continuous at }\bm{t}\}\cup\{\bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{l}:\gradient{f}(\bm{t})=0\}$ . By assumption, the closure of $Q$ , which we denote as $\overline{Q}$ , has Lebesgue measure $0$ . Let $\bm{y}\in P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}$ , Since $\overline{Q}$ is closed, and $\bm{y}$ is in the complement of $\overline{Q}$ , there must exist an open neighborhood of $\bm{y}$ that is in $\mathbb{R}^{l}\setminus\overline{Q}$ . Also there must be at least one element of $\gradient f(\bm{y})$ that is not zero, again, because $\bm{y}$ is in the complement of $\overline{Q}$ . Without loss of generality, assume that the last element of $\gradient f(\bm{y})$ is nonzero, i.e., $\gradient f(\bm{y})_{l}\neq 0$ . Then, by the Implicit Function Theorem (Theorem 3.1, Folland (2002)), there exists open sets $U_{\bm{y}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{l-1}$ and $V_{\bm{y}}\subset\mathbb{R}$ such that $(y_{1},...,y_{l-1})\in U_{\bm{y}}$ and $y_{l}\in V_{\bm{y}}$ and there exists a unique function $g:U_{\bm{y}}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\{y_{1},...,y_{l-1},g(y_{1},...,y_{l-1}):(y_{1},...,y_{l-1})\in U_{\bm{y}}\} \displaystyle=\{\bm{y}\in U_{\bm{y}}\times V_{\bm{y}}\mid f(\bm{y})=x\} \displaystyle=P_{x}\cap\left(U_{\bm{y}}\times V_{\bm{y}}\right) $$

and $g$ is continuously differentiable. In the above, $\times$ represents the Cartesian product. Let $W_{\bm{y}}=U_{\bm{y}}\times V_{\bm{y}}$ . Note, $\{y_{1},...,y_{l-1},g(y_{1},...,y_{l-1}):(y_{1},...,y_{l-1})\in U_{\bm{y}}\}$ is the graph of the continuous function $g:U_{\bm{y}}\to\mathbb{R}$ , and so has Lebesgue measure $0$ in $\mathbb{R}^{l}$ (Proposition 6.3, Lee (2003)). Therefore, $\forall\bm{y}\in P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}$ , there exists an open set $W_{\bm{y}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that

$$ \mu\left(P_{x}\cap W_{\bm{y}}\right)=0. $$

We can write

$$ \displaystyle P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}=\bigcup_{\bm{y}\in P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}}\left(P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\right)\cap W_{\bm{y}}=\left(P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\right)\cap\left(\bigcup_{\bm{y}\in P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}}W_{\bm{y}}\right). $$

Note, $\bigcup_{y\in P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}}W_{\bm{y}}$ is a open cover of $P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{l}$ . By the fact that $\mathbb{R}^{l}$ is second-countable (Example 1.2, Wedhorn (2016)), and any subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{l}$ is second-countable (Remark 1.3, Wedhorn (2016)), by Lindelöf’s Covering Theorem (Theorem 15, Kelley (1955)), there exists a countable subcover of $P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}$ , i.e., for some countable set $A\in P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}$ , $P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\subseteq\bigcup_{\bm{y}\in A}W_{\bm{y}}.$ Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\cap\left(\bigcup_{\bm{y}\in P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}}W_{\bm{y}}\right) \displaystyle=P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\cap\left(\bigcup_{\bm{y}\in A}W_{\bm{y}}\right)=\bigcup_{\bm{y}\in A}\left(P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\right)\cap W_{\bm{y}} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mu\left(\bigcup_{\bm{y}\in A}\left(P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\right)\cap W_{\bm{y}}\right)\leq\sum_{\bm{y}\in A}\mu\left(\left(P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\right)\cap W_{\bm{y}}\right)\leq\sum_{\bm{y}\in A}\mu\left(P_{x}\cap W_{\bm{y}}\right)=0. $$

The last equality follows from Equation (20) and the fact that $A$ is a countable set.

Therefore, $\mu\left(P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\right)=0$ and

$$ \mu(P_{x})\leq\mu\left(\left(P_{x}\setminus\overline{Q}\right)\cup\overline{Q}\right)=0 $$

Since we picked $x$ to be any arbitrary element of $R_{f}$ , the above is true for all $x\in R_{f}$ . ∎

## Appendix G Approximate Validity of the Unadjusted cPCH Test

We find that, under the setting in Section 2.1, for a fixed $m$ , $r$ , and $\alpha$ , the unadjusted cPCH test has small and quantifiable Type I error inflation. Additionally, we find that for a fixed $m$ and $r$ , the unadjusted cPCH test produces nearly uniform p-values under the null. Thus, we call the unadjusted cPCH test “approximately valid and non-conservative”.

Our characterization of the unadjusted cPCH test’s validity for finite $\theta_{i}$ relies fundamentally on the fact that, for a given choice of $m$ and $r$ , we can estimate the unadjusted cPCH p-value distribution for a given $\bm{\theta}\in\Theta_{0}^{r/m}$ with high accuracy via Monte Carlo sampling. Specifically, given a $\bm{\theta}\in\Theta_{0}^{r/m}$ , we generate samples $\tilde{\bm{T}}^{(k)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i.i.d}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}({\bm{\theta}},I_{m}),k=1,...,N$ and compute the unadjusted cPCH p-value for each sample to empirically estimate the distribution of the unadjusted cPCH p-value under $\bm{\theta}$ . Performing this sampling procedure across a sufficiently fine grid of $\Theta_{0}^{r/m}$ with many replicates $N$ allows us to obtain highly accurate estimates of the p-value distribution under the null for the desired $m$ and $r$ . Given a fixed $\alpha$ , we can also use the Monte Carlo samples to obtain highly accurate estimates of the Type I error for each $\bm{\theta}\in\Theta_{0}^{r/m}$ by computing the proportion of the sampled cPCH p-values at $\bm{\theta}\in\Theta_{0}^{r/m}$ that are below $\alpha$ .

We pause to highlight that our approach in this section is somewhat different from a usual simulation study, which would typically explore a small (but hopefully at least somewhat representative) subset of all possible data-generating scenarios. In contrast, we provide an exhaustive characterization of the unadjusted cPCH p-value distribution at effectively every null $\bm{\theta}$ for realistic values of $m$ and $r$ . Such an exhaustive search is made possible by the small dimension of the null space for most common PCH testing scenarios, such as causal mediation analysis, where $m=2$ , and replicability analysis, where $m$ is often $\leq 5$ Bogomolov and Heller (2013); Heller and Yekutieli (2014); Wang et al. (2021). For all analyses in this section, we fix $\alpha=0.05$ . Thus, the following results can be interpreted as a computational proof that, for the configurations of $m$ and $r$ tested, the cPCH test produces approximately uniform p-values under the null and that, for $\alpha=0.05$ , the Type I error inflation of the cPCH test is small. We expect these results to generalize to larger $m$ and different choices of $\alpha$ . Though our results assume the setting of Section 2.1 where each $T_{i}$ are single, independent unit-variance Gaussians, our simulations in Section C suggest that the following results would still hold under other distributional assumptions for the base test statistics.

## Appendix H PCH Multiple Testing Simulation Study

In this section, we present the full details of the PCH multiple testing simulation study summarized in Section 4.2. Recall, we assume there are $M$ PCH’s being simultaneously tested and denote $T_{ij}$ and $p_{ij}$ as the $i$ th base test statistic and p-value, respectively, for the $j$ th PCH being tested, $i=1,...,m$ , $j=1,...,M$ .

### H.1 An Overview of Methods Under Comparison

Our study includes two state-of-the-art Empirical Bayes methods, the Divide-Aggregate Composite-null Test (DACT) Liu et al. (2022) and High Dimensional Multiple Testing (HDMT) Dai et al. (2020) and two state-of-the-art filtering methods, AdaFilter Wang et al. (2021) and the method presented in Dickhaus et al. (2023).

Both DACT and HDMT adapt existing empirical Bayes frameworks for estimating the proportion of each null configuration Efron et al. (2001); Storey (2002); Storey et al. (2004). They both guarantee FDR control as $M\to\infty$ under specific regularity conditions, which are primarily set to guarantee that the estimators for the proportions of each null configuration are consistent. Additionally, by the linear structural model commonly used for causal mediation analysis Baron and Kenny (1986), both DACT and HDMT assume that the base test statistics are normally distributed and independent across $m$ . The primary difference between DACT and HDMT (and Empirical Bayes methods in general) lies in how the estimated proportions are used. DACT generates individual PCH p-values that are weighted sums of the estimated proportions of each null configuration, on which FDR controlling procedures like BH can be applied. HDMT estimates the FDR of the Max-P test at a given rejection threshold using these proportions, then selects the largest rejection threshold such that the estimated FDR is less than or equal to the desired level. Importantly, both HDMT and DACT are designed for causal mediation analysis, a specific case of PCH testing with $r=m=2$ , and thus, are only applicable (as implemented) when $m=2$ . However, the statistical frameworks used by Empirical Bayes methods for estimating the proportions of the null configurations are not limited to the $m=2$ case and thus, these methods could reasonably be extended to larger $m$ . As the computational cost of Empirical Bayes methods can grow exponentially in $m$ Wang et al. (2021), fixing $r=m=2$ allows Empirical Bayes methods to produce accurate estimates of the true proportions within reasonable computational limits, as long as $M$ is sufficiently large and the conditions necessary for the consistency of their estimators are met.

AdaFilter is a filtering method that infers a new (ideally less conservative) rejection threshold in a data-adaptive manner. It first reduces the set of total PCH’s to the subset that would be rejected by Bonferroni PCH tests for $H_{0}^{(r-1)/m}$ , then applies an adjusted version of the Bonferroni PCH test for $H_{0}^{r/m}$ to each PCH in the reduced set. Intuitively, this filtering is effective because the null PCH’s that are rejected for $H_{0}^{(r-1)/m}$ are close to the LFN, so the Bonferroni PCH test will be less conservative on the reduced set. Under mild regularity conditions, AdaFilter guarantees FDR control as $M\to\infty$ . For finite $M$ and nominal FDR level $q$ , AdaFilter guarantees FDR control at level $qC(M)$ where $C(M)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1}{j}$ , when all $p_{ij}$ are independent.

DHH filters out all PCH p-values $p^{r/m}$ above some threshold $\tau$ , then applies a transformation to the smaller subset so that, under mild conditions on the $p_{ij}$ and $p^{r/m}$ , various FDR controlling procedures such as BH and Storey’s procedure can be applied to the smaller subset to control FDR on the entire set. Thus, there are many variations of DHH depending on the PCH p-value and multiple testing procedure used. In our analysis, we use PCH p-values from Simes’ and Fisher’s tests, which are shown in Dickhaus et al. (2023) to satisfy the conditions necessary for the DHH procedure (with fixed $\tau$ ) to have FDR control when using BH or Storey’s procedure. Dickhaus et al. (2023) also provides an algorithm for selecting the threshold $\tau$ in a data-adaptive way, which, under certain conditions, guarantees asymptotic FDR control. We select $\tau=0.1$ since, as shown in the empirical simulations and real data example presented in Dickhaus et al. (2023), DHH with $\tau=0.1$ has similar power to DHH with the data-adaptive threshold in many settings.

For all PCH multiple testing approaches under consideration (DACT, HDMT, AdaFilter, and DHH), their FDR guarantees hold under the assumption that the $p_{ij}$ are independent, or some mild relaxation of it (e.g., AdaFilter allows weak dependence between the base p-values for their asymptotic results). Thus, for all following simulations, we generate data such that the $p_{ij}$ are independent.

For methods which generate individual p-values such as the cPCH test, we focus on three FDR controlling procedures: Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) Benjamini and Hochberg (1995), Storey’s Storey et al. (2004), and AdaPT–GMM Chao and Fithian (2021). Note, since DACT and DHH produce individual PCH p-values (though they rely on being in a PCH multiple testing setting to do so), we also combine them with the procedures above. We now discuss the assumptions necessary for FDR control for these procedures. Storey’s procedure and AdaPT–GMM share the assumption that the individual PCH p-values are independent, while BH only requires positive regression dependency on a subset. AdaPT–GMM requires the additional assumption that the null p-values have a non-decreasing density. The standard PCH p-values and DHH-adjusted PCH p-values satisfy the non-decreasing density condition, while DACT and cPCH p-values are not guaranteed to do so. However, since null cPCH p-values are nearly uniform, the non-decreasing density assumption is at least justified approximately for the cPCH test. Additionally, we find in our empirical simulations that FDR control is maintained when using cPCH p-values with AdaPT–GMM. In all simulations, we include the standard Simes’ and Fisher’s tests for single PCH testing in combination with BH, Storey’s procedure, and AdaPT–GMM (when applicable) as benchmarks for comparison.

### H.3 PCH Multiple Testing for $m=4$

To approximate the real-data example in the following section, we conduct a simulation study to assess the empirical FDR and power of various PCH multiple testing approaches when $m=4$ and $M=2000$ . As we explore a few different testing scenarios in our real data example, we choose a data generating procedure that allows us to flexibly vary the proportion of null and alternative configurations, thus emulating a wide range of possible testing scenarios for $m=4$ and $M=2000$ . We generate the data $T_{ij}$ , $i=1,...,4$ , $j=1,..,2000$ by sampling independently from the following model:

$$ \displaystyle B_{j} \displaystyle\sim\text{Bern}(\pi_{1}) \displaystyle\gamma_{ij}|B_{j} \displaystyle\sim\begin{cases}B_{j}&\text{w/p }w\\
\text{Bern}(\pi_{1})&\text{w/p }1-w\\
\end{cases} \displaystyle T_{ij}|\gamma_{ij},B_{j} \displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\theta\gamma_{ij},1) $$

$\pi_{1}$ tunes the expected proportion of the null and alternative PCH’s and $p$ tunes the likelihood of each null and alternative configuration. For example, when $w=1$ , we expect $\pi_{1}$ of the total PCH’s to be alternatives, all of which are “full alternatives” (i.e., $r^{\star}=m$ ), and all remaining PCH’s to be global nulls.

Discoveries are generated using AdaFilter, the cPCH test ( $N=10,000$ ), the standard Simes and Fisher tests, and DHH ( $\tau=0.1$ ), each with BH and Storey’s procedures. All procedures are applied at nominal FDR level $q=0.1$ . The Empirical Bayes methods under consideration focus on the $m=2$ case and hence cannot be applied in this setting.

*Figure 16: False Discovery Rate (FDR) results corresponding to Section H.3 where all methods are implemented at nominal level $q=0.1$ (dotted black line). Each point represents the average proportion of rejected PCH’s which are null over $1000$ independent replicates of the data generating procedure described in Section H.3 for a given $\theta$ . Standard errors were all less than $0.008$ .*

We show that all methods under consideration empirically control the FDR at the nominal level for every combination of $\theta,\pi_{1}$ , and $w$ tested; see Figure 16. Note, finite-sample FDR control is guaranteed with the Max-P test (with BH and Storey’s procedure) and DHH (with BH and Storey’s procedure). These results, along with those of the previous section, suggest that AdaFilter and the cPCH–based approaches, neither of which guaranteed FDR control at level $q$ in this setting, have robust FDR control across a wide array of testing settings. As shown in Figure 17, we find that the relative power of these methods is highly sensitive to the underlying data generating distribution, so no method dominates all others across all settings. However, the cPCH test is more powerful than its standard counterparts in all data generating settings. As expected, we see that the AdaFilter and DHH methods have the highest power when $\pi_{1}$ is small, as the construction of filtering methods allows them to be especially effective in this setting. For instance, DHH is likely to significantly reduce the multiplicity of PCH’s being tested as a vast majority of the PCH p-values will be above $\tau$ .

As we alluded to in Section 1.4, even the standard single PCH tests with BH and Storey’s procedure can outperform DHH and AdaFilter in this setting. There are various important applications where $\pi_{1}$ is expected to be large. For instance, in epigenetics, promising sets of candidate genes from pre-screening studies or prior knowledge are often re-evaluated in follow-up studies O’Donovan et al. (2008); Benjamini et al.
